afanasievo-culture.name: Afanasievo culture
afanasievo-culture.summary: An early archaeological culture of south Siberia's Minusinsk Basin and Altai Mountains, dated about 3300 to 2500 BCE, whose people migrated there from the Volga-Ural region, with burials found as far as central Mongolia.

altai-mountains.name: Altai Mountains
altai-mountains.summary: Mountain range in Central Asia where Russia, China, Mongolia, and Kazakhstan meet, home to a sparse, ethnically diverse population including Turkic peoples and Mongols.

botai-culture.name: Botai culture
botai-culture.summary: A prehistoric archaeological culture (c. 3700–3100 BC) in what is now northern Kazakhstan, named after its settlement, with evidence suggesting early domestication of horses.

kelteminar-culture.name: Kelteminar culture
kelteminar-culture.summary: A Neolithic culture of sedentary fishermen (5500–3500 BCE) in the deserts of what are now Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, discovered in 1939 by Soviet archaeologists.

amu-darya.name: Amu Darya
amu-darya.summary: A major Central Asian river, historically called the Oxus, that flows through Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan and was once seen as the boundary between Greater Iran and Turan.

zarafshon-river.name: Zeravshan River
zarafshon-river.summary: A river flowing through Tajikistan and Uzbekistan whose Persian name means 'spreader of gold', for gold-bearing sands upstream; ancient Greeks called it the Polytimetus.

idel-ural.name: Volga-Ural region
idel-ural.summary: A historical region in Eastern Europe around the Volga and Ural rivers, in what is today Russia, now encompassing six republics including Tatarstan and Bashkortostan.

hisar-range.name: Hisar Range
hisar-range.summary: A mountain range in Central Asia, in the western Pamir-Alay system, stretching over 200 km across Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

przewalski-s-horse.name: Przewalski's horse
przewalski-s-horse.summary: A rare, endangered wild horse native to the Central Asian steppes, named after Russian explorer Nikolay Przhevalsky; once extinct in the wild, it has been reintroduced to Mongolia since the 1990s.

banpo.name: Banpo
banpo.summary: A Neolithic site in China's Yellow River valley, representing the first phase of the Yangshao culture (c. 5000-3000 BCE), with circular mud-and-wood houses and communal burials.

bolshemys-culture.name: Bolshemys culture
bolshemys-culture.summary: An Eneolithic culture (4000–3000 BCE) of foot hunters in Siberia's Altai mountains, known for thin-walled pottery with jagged-line and comb-pattern decoration.

karakum-desert.name: Karakum Desert
karakum-desert.summary: The 12th largest desert in the world, covering about 70 percent of Turkmenistan, sparsely populated and receiving very little rainfall.

kyzylkum-desert.name: Kyzylkum Desert
kyzylkum-desert.summary: A large Central Asian desert, the 15th largest in the world, lying between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers and now divided among Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

ishim-river.name: Ishim River
ishim-river.summary: A 2,450-kilometre river flowing through Kazakhstan and Russia, a left tributary of the Irtysh; its upper course passes through Astana, Kazakhstan's capital.

ust-belaya.name: Ust-Belaya
ust-belaya.summary: A small Siberian village in Chukotka, Russia, at the confluence of the Anadyr and Belaya Rivers, where an ancient walrus-hunting grave was excavated.

chukotka-autonomous-okrug.name: Chukotka
chukotka-autonomous-okrug.summary: The easternmost federal subject of Russia, bordering the Bering Strait opposite Alaska and home to ethnic Chukchi and other indigenous peoples.

yamnaya-culture.name: Yamnaya culture
yamnaya-culture.summary: A Copper to early Bronze Age culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe (3300–2600 BC), known for pit-grave burials under kurgans and often linked to Proto-Indo-European origins.

pontic-caspian-steppe.name: Pontic–Caspian Steppe
pontic-caspian-steppe.summary: A vast grassland stretching from the northern Black Sea to the Caspian Sea, corresponding to ancient Scythia and Sarmatia, and thought to be where horses were first domesticated.

kent-flannery.name: Kent Flannery
kent-flannery.summary: American archaeologist, born 1934, known for proposing the Broad Spectrum Revolution and for influential research on the origins of agriculture in Mesoamerica and the Near East.

south-caucasus.name: Transcaucasia
south-caucasus.summary: Also called the South Caucasus, a region on the southern Caucasus Mountains roughly matching modern Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan.

tyumen-oblast.name: Tyumen Oblast
tyumen-oblast.summary: A federal subject of Russia in Western Siberia, one of the country's largest regions by area and its leading producer of oil and natural gas.

ancient-north-eurasian.name: Ancient North Eurasian
ancient-north-eurasian.summary: An ancestral genetic lineage tracing to the Mal'ta–Buret' culture in Siberia around 24,000 years ago, formed from a mix of ancient West and East Eurasian peoples.

sarazm.name: Sarazm
sarazm.summary: An ancient town and archaeological site in northwestern Tajikistan dating to the 4th millennium BC, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site that predates the region's steppe cultures.

david-w-anthony.name: David W. Anthony
david-w-anthony.summary: American anthropologist specializing in horse domestication and Indo-European migrations, known for his book The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007).

minusinsk-hollow.name: Minusinsk Hollow
minusinsk-hollow.summary: A basin in Khakassia and Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia, situated among the mountains of southern Siberia.

repin-culture.name: Repin culture
repin-culture.summary: A 4th-millennium BCE Eneolithic culture of the Pontic-Caspian steppe that grew from local Neolithic groups and later developed into the Yamnaya culture, based on pastoralism and hunting.

namazga-tepe.name: Namazga-Depe
namazga-tepe.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological site in Turkmenistan whose excavations established the chronology used for the region's Bronze Age sites.

altyndepe.name: Altyn-Depe
altyndepe.summary: Bronze Age archaeological site in Turkmenistan, inhabited from about 3200 to 2000 BC, that grew into a full urban settlement by its later period.

marghab-river.name: Marghab River
marghab-river.summary: An 850-kilometre river in Central Asia rising in the Paropamisus Mountains that flows northwest through Afghanistan into the Karakum Desert, reaching the oasis of Mary in Turkmenistan.

panjakent.name: Panjakent
panjakent.summary: A city in modern Tajikistan on the river Zeravshan, once an ancient town in Sogdiana, with old-town ruins near the modern city.

lake-baikal.name: Lake Baikal
lake-baikal.summary: The world's deepest lake, in southern Siberia, Russia, and the largest freshwater lake by volume, estimated to be 25 to 30 million years old.

microlith.name: Microlith
microlith.summary: A small stone tool, usually flint or chert, made by humans since at least the Upper Paleolithic across Africa, Europe, Asia and Australia to tip spears and arrows.

khakassia.name: Khakassia
khakassia.summary: A republic of Russia in southern Siberia, with its capital at Abakan, known for its rivers, mountains, and the Khakassky Nature Reserve.

sergei-teploukhov.name: Sergei Teploukhov
sergei-teploukhov.summary: Soviet archaeologist (1888–1934) who researched Siberia and Central Asia from 1920 to 1932 and first classified the archaeological cultures of Southern Siberia.

tamaz-v-gamkrelidze.name: Tamaz Gamkrelidze
tamaz-v-gamkrelidze.summary: Georgian linguist, orientalist and Hittitologist (1929–2021) who led the Georgian Academy of Sciences as president from 2005 to 2013.

yeniseian-languages.name: Yeniseian languages
yeniseian-languages.summary: A family of languages spoken by the Yeniseian people of central Siberia, of which only Ket survives; evidence suggests they once covered a much wider area, including parts of northern China and Mongolia.

v-clav-bla-ek.name: Václav Blažek
v-clav-bla-ek.summary: Czech historical linguist (born 1959), professor at Masaryk University, specializing in Indo-European, Uralic, Altaic and other Eurasian language families.

proto-indo-european-language.name: Proto-Indo-European language
proto-indo-european-language.summary: The reconstructed common ancestor of all Indo-European languages, likely spoken from about 4500 to 2500 BCE, possibly originating in the Pontic-Caspian steppe.
